tools.title: Did Democrats blow it in Florida?
tools.summary_raw: Democrats came close in the Sunshine State. But in a national blue tsunami, should they have done better?
tools.content_text: Angie Nixon speaking at a rally in Kissimmee, Florida. Joe Raedle/Getty Images. Eight years ago, Democrats retook the U.S. House, netting 41 seats and winning the national popular vote by 8.6 points in a textbook blue wave. But despite the rosy national environment, Republican Rick Scott narrowly defeated incumbent Democratic Senator Bill Nelson in Florida. In hindsight, that victory, on the heels of Donald Trump’s 2016 win in the state, was the harbinger of a death spiral for Florida Democrats that had begun years earlier. When I wrote about the Sunshine State back in February , the consensus from both prediction markets and the experts I spoke with was that Democrats were highly unlikely to win the state in 2026. After a decade of losses and underinvestment, it looked like it could take another ten years for Democrats to turn Florida purple again. The short-term goal of the Florida Democratic Party (FDP) was less “win the 2026 Senate race” and more “ get out of the superminority in the state legislature .” But back then, no one knew that 2026 would be a blue tsunami where Democrats would win the national popular vote by 13 points and net nine Senate seats. 1 And yet they still lost both statewide races in Florida. Almost immediately, people started posting post-election recriminations that if Democrats had spent more in Florida, they could have pulled off at least one win. So did Democrats blow a golden opportunity in Florida? Or is the state still too tough a target? That question should weigh on the party because in two short years, Ashley Moody will be up for re-election . Read more

tools.title: Silver Bulletin is hiring an editor and a developer
tools.content_text: Silver Bulletin is hiring a Deputy Editor and an Associate Interactive Developer . The Deputy Editor is a full-time role for someone with editing experience in journalism or a closely related field and a strong interest in our major beats, which include politics (especially elections), sports, and AI. We envision the Associate Interactive Developer role as initially part-time and open to candidates early in their careers. We would consider a full-time and/or more experienced hire for an exceptional candidate who can persuade us of the value they’d bring to the site. The deadline to apply for both positions is 5 p.m. ET on Friday, December 18. We’ll begin reviewing materials and interviewing candidates in early January and don’t expect to contact applicants before the deadline. Interviews will be conducted by video or in person. Even if the jobs aren’t a good fit for you, we’d encourage you to circulate these listings to people who might be interested. Silver Bulletin is an equal opportunity employer. We welcome applicants from all backgrounds provided they are eligible to work in the United States. Silver Bulletin is growing as a business and maturing as a site. Our newsletters and models typically reach hundreds of thousands to millions of readers. The economics of the business are sound, and we hope these will be long-term roles with growth potential for ambitious candidates. We want to make our coverage more robust, improving both quality and quantity in the areas where our subscribers already really like our coverage. We’re looking for hires who have opinions about the strengths and shortcomings of the site and ideas about how to make it better. Our current four-person team works incredibly hard, but we’re overstretched. We want a couple of new voices in the room to help us do more for our readers. We use AI tools for tasks such as copy editing and helping code our models, but writing at Silver Bulletin is done by human hands. Beyond assistance with standard copy editing and formatting, you should disclose any use of AI in completing your application. Deputy Editor The Deputy Editor job requires strong people skills and an understanding of both our journalism and our business. Although this isn’t the only metric for success, we’d like to publish about one additional high-quality story per week. Job tasks Edit work from Silver Bulletin staff and freelancers. This will often include “nose-to-tail” editing: working with the writers to develop the story, sharpen the argument, and improve the precision of the published piece. Help develop our editorial plan from day to day and week to week. Plan around the demands of the news cycle, weighing the trade-offs between responsiveness and depth. Develop a group of paid freelancers to add coverage on our main beats, with a particular emphasis on building out our AI coverage. Consider logical areas for expansion, such as economics, finance, tech, and public policy. […]

market.title: “A healthy degree of vitality”: Medill takes a look at the Twin Cities’ local news ecosystem
market.summary_raw: This year’s State of Local News Report from Medill was grim. But in the Twin Cities, Neal St. Anthony writes, a rich local news ecosystem offers a more hopeful picture. The metro area of more than 3 million people is home to The Minnesota Star Tribune, public radio powerhouse MPR, local TV stations, and multiple...
market.content_text: This year’s State of Local News Report from Medill was grim . But in the Twin Cities, Neal St. Anthony writes , a rich local news ecosystem offers a more hopeful picture. The metro area of more than 3 million people is home to The Minnesota Star Tribune, public radio powerhouse MPR, local TV stations, and multiple successful nonprofit startups, from nearly two-decade-old MinnPost to Sahan Journal (whose founder, Mukhtar Ibrahim, also launched The Somali Brief this fall). Axios has published an Axios Local newsletter for the Twin Cities since 2021, and this summer , The New York Times launched its own Twin Cities local newsletter. The question this ecosystem raises, according to St. Anthony, is “whether the Twin Cities represents the potential future of local news in metros across the country: a robust ecosystem with no dominant mass-market player but more news outlets tailored to smaller, niche audiences with narrower but deep interests.” (That description brings to mind other urban media markets where a diffuse ecosystem of smaller, newer players have stepped up as legacy media pulls back.) “There is a healthy degree of vitality in local news in the Twin Cities. The story elsewhere is ‘news deserts’ and little original journalism,” University of Minnesota professor Benjamin Toff told St. Anthony. While local institutions like the Star Tribune have survived, he added, “it’s not immune to industry forces, including the veritable disappearance of print.” A few highlights from St. Anthony’s piece for Medill: On the Star Tribune : The Strib had about 107,000 digital subscribers as of August, up 30% since 2021, while daily print circulation fell 65% over that period, to 57,000. “Our digital subscription business has grown 25% since 2024. We’re trying things. Some will work. We must diversify our revenue streams, including philanthropy,” CEO Steve Grove told St. Anthony. The Star Tribune is exploring converting to a nonprofit . A fund launched at the Minneapolis Foundation in 2024 in support of the Star Tribune has raised about $1 million to date. St. Anthony reports the Strib’s sponsored content initiative has attracted more than 60 advertisers. Meanwhile, it’s offering subscribers a free 12-month subscription to The New York Times. On MPR : After the 2025 rescission of federal funding for public media, Minnesota Public Radio lost about $6 million. But MPR, like other public broadcasters, was able to turn the rescission into a highly successful fundraising campaign. Its 2026 fiscal revenue rose 5% to $119 million, and it grew to 172,000 paying members, a record. On Axios Local : Holly Moore, executive editor of Axios Local, called Twin Cities a “successful market.” She told St. Anthony Axios Local has about 2.5 million free subscribers across its 43 markets, adding, “We want to create a sustainable business model. We are largely ad sales.” Read the full story here .

market.content_text: Is something in the water in Nieman Lab’s home state? In our latest quarterly ranking of nonprofit news outlets, eight Massachusetts nonprofit news outlets enjoyed significant jumps in traffic. Massachusetts is the state that appeared most frequently in this quarter’s data, followed by California (7), Michigan (4), and New York (4). Four of those Massachusetts outlets largely attributed the traffic spikes to hyperlocal stories that served specific reader needs and curiosities. Cambridge Day garnered 160,000 visits in July, a 60% increase from June. Editor Michael Fitzgerald (a 2011 Nieman Fellow) said the publication’s top story that month was about the city halting a multifamily home demolition. Other big stories covered the sale of two independent movie theaters and a July 4 shooting . Reader support allowed Cambridge Day to hire a full-time reporter in June, along with four summer intern reporters whose positions were funded through their universities. In July, Fitzgerald said, the news outlet published 32 stories per week. “Having full-time reporters was transformative. News does not pay a living wage to freelancers,” Fitzgerald said in an email. “They have to pay their bills by doing other things, so they just aren’t as available as full-time reporters. We made the decision to hire a second reporter, who started in late August. We took a bit of a risk and brought on [a] freelancer as a six-month editorial fellow. I cut my freelance budget in half and have rejiggered some other expenses to make this less risky.” The Lexington Observer got 62,000 visits in August, a 47% increase from the previous month. Executive director Lauren Feeney said the August story with the most traffic was about how a resident-led complaint delayed the construction of what would be the most expensive high school in the country. Election coverage ahead of the midterms also resonated. “ Our coverage of two little-known progressive candidates running to unseat [Rep. Katherine Clark] from the left got a ton of traffic, I believe because hardly anything else had been written about them, so readers came to our site not just from Lexington but from the entire 5th Congressional district, including Cambridge,” Feeney said. “My takeaway from this is to keep focusing on undercovered and hyperlocal stories, and not spend a lot of resources on stories that are already widely covered.” August was also a newsy month for the Marblehead Current . With 156 published stories in August, the Current’s traffic increased by 53% compared to July. Cofounder and reporter Leigh Blander said her investigation into the city’s road conditions sparked engagement on Facebook and Instagram, driving pageviews. Other stories that resonated with readers covered a boat crash , a seal carcass , racist graffiti , and education coverage during back-to-school season. CommonWealth Beacon , which covers statewide politics and policy, saw its September traffic increase by 37% over August. […]
